title: Standard Continuous Distributions
objectives: Identify support and parameterisation of the main continuous distribution families.
Compute probabilities from PDFs, CDFs and survival functions.
Distinguish exponential and gamma rate from scale conventions.
Calculate means and variances for uniform, exponential, gamma, beta and normal laws.
Recognise chi-square, t and F distributions and their parameter roles.

prereq.name: Gamma and beta functions
prereq.why: Evaluate Gamma and Beta normalising constants.

traps: Identify support before choosing a family.
For exponential rate λ, mean=1/λ; for scale θ, mean=θ.
Gamma rate and scale are reciprocals.
Beta is supported on (0,1); Gamma and chi-square on (0,∞).
For continuous X, P(X=x)=0 even if f(x)>0.
F degrees of freedom are ordered: numerator first, denominator second.

sheet: Exp(rate λ): mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ², survival e^(−λx).
Gamma(shape α, rate λ): mean α/λ, variance α/λ².
tricks: Read rate or scale before using a formula.
Support usually identifies the family quickly.
For integer Gamma shape use Erlang survival sums.
remember: A density value is not a point probability.

howto: Identify support first, then match the density kernel and parameter convention. Work the Gamma survival example and Beta tail integral, then practise rate-versus-scale conversions. A density value is not a point probability.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four foundations
body: A continuous law is identified by support, density and parameters.
The main exam traps are rate versus scale, support limits and confusing a density value with a point probability.

ask.q: What is P(X=x) for an absolutely continuous variable?
ask.nudge: A density is not a point mass.

refresh: Write the support and density or pmf before choosing a distribution formula. A discrete variable has point probabilities that sum to one; a continuous variable has a density whose integral is one. Check the parameter convention carefully, especially whether a geometric variable counts trials or failures and whether a negative binomial counts successes or failures.

items.recall: F(b)−F(a), or integrate f from a to b.
refresh: For a binomial variable, identify a fixed number n of independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability p. Its mean is np and variance np(1−p). Do not use this model when the number of trials is random or success probabilities differ across trials.

For a Poisson variable, λ is both the mean and variance and represents the expected count over the stated interval or exposure. Independent Poisson counts add, with parameters adding. If the interval or exposure is multiplied by c under a constant rate, the parameter becomes cλ.

items.ask: What is the Gamma function at an integer n?
refresh: For a continuous uniform variable on (a,b), the density is 1/(b−a), the mean is (a+b)/2 and the variance is (b−a)²/12. For exponential rate λ, the mean is 1/λ and variance 1/λ²; distinguish rate from scale before substituting.

scenes.title: Support and parameterisation come first
scenes.objective: Use support and rate/scale to identify the family.
body: The support often narrows the possible family before any calculation. A proportion lives on (0,1); a waiting time lives on (0,∞); a normal variable can take any real value.
For exponential and Gamma laws, rate and scale are reciprocals. Writing the density before using a parameter prevents the most common factor error.

scenario.teaser: A call-centre manager mistakes an exponential rate for its mean.
scenario.title: Rate and scale reverse the answer
body: A waiting time is exponential with rate λ=4 per hour. A report states that the average wait is four hours.
Under the rate convention, the mean is 1/λ=0.25 hours, or fifteen minutes. The survival probability beyond half an hour is e^(−4×.5)=e^(−2)=0.1353.
If written with scale θ, then θ=1/λ=.25 hours and the density is θ⁻¹e^(−x/θ). Rate and scale are reciprocals.
Write the density before substituting a parameter. It reveals whether the given parameter is a rate or scale.
scenario.q: For Exp(rate 4), what are the mean and P(X>.5)?

ask.q: Why should you write the density before substituting λ?
ask.nudge: It tells you whether λ multiplies x in the exponent or divides it.

blocks.body: f(x)=1/(b−a), a<x<b; E(X)=(a+b)/2; Var(X)=(b−a)²/12. Probabilities are interval lengths divided by b−a.
f(x)=λe^(−λx), x≥0; P(X>x)=e^(−λx); mean=1/λ and variance=1/λ². Scale θ=1/λ.
f(x)=λ^αx^(α−1)e^(−λx)/Γ(α); mean=α/λ, variance=α/λ². With scale θ, mean=αθ.
Standardise Z=(X−μ)/σ. Linear combinations of jointly normal variables remain normal.
χ²_ν is Gamma(ν/2, rate 1/2); t_ν=Z/√(U/ν); F_{ν1,ν2}=(U₁/ν₁)/(U₂/ν₂), independent chi-squares.

blocks.body: χ²_ν is Gamma(shape ν/2, rate 1/2); mean ν and variance 2ν.
t_ν=Z/√(U/ν), where Z~N(0,1), U~χ²_ν and they are independent.
F_{ν₁,ν₂}=(U₁/ν₁)/(U₂/ν₂), with independent chi-squares. The numerator df is written first.

scenario.teaser: A reliability analyst must distinguish Gamma from Beta by support and kernel.
scenario.title: Support is the first clue
body: A lifetime is positive and has density proportional to x²e^(−2x). The power identifies Gamma shape 3; the exponential term identifies rate 2.
A proportion is bounded between zero and one and has density proportional to x(1−x)². That is Beta(2,3).
Both can be skewed, but their supports differ: Gamma lives on (0,∞), Beta on (0,1).
For exam questions identify support first, match the kernel second, and check the normalising constant and parameter convention last.
scenario.q: Which family has support (0,1) and density proportional to x(1−x)²?

solution.why: Integrate the stated density over the upper half.

items.claim: For Exp(rate λ), the mean is λ.
The Beta distribution is supported on (0,1).
items.why: True: its density is defined on the unit interval.

items.claim: Gamma(shape α, rate λ) has mean α/λ.
items.why: True: the rate is in the denominator.

items.claim: A probability density may exceed one.
items.why: True: density is probability per unit length.
False: point probability is zero; f(x) is a density.

items.claim: For F_{ν1,ν2}, ν1 is numerator degrees of freedom.
items.why: True: numerator df is written first.
